newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - bulls may be ready for more.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - bulls may be ready for more.

text.p: U.S. crude oil prices may be positioned for some more gains after breaking technical restraints last week, when prompt barrels pushed above the $22.00 mark, crude traders said.

The market, however, will remain choppy early in the week as players roll out of June NYMEX futures contract ahead of Tuesday's expiry with the fundamental picture over the next couple of months a bit unclear, traders said.

Cash crude players were even more on edge for expiry due to some forecasts calling for a repeat of May, when a huge 2.73 million barrel load of foreign barrels was delivered against the NYMEX contract.
Even though most domestic cash players were not looking for the same huge numbers of foreign deliveries, there were calls for as much as one million barrels of fresh delivery.
"You're hearing the talk, people expecting big deliveries. But, the question is who is going to let themselves get delivered against. I can't believe it will be many," said a Texas cash broker.

Many refiners purchased an insurance policy against getting stuck with uneconomic foreign barrels in the form of exchange for physical (EFP's) contracts, guaranteeing West Texas Intermediate/Cushing for their pipelines.

"EFP's are around five to seven cents now, and the last heard done was at seven cents (premium to the futures contract)," said a trader, noting EFP values have shrunk in the last week on slowing demand.
"Anyone who was going to buy has done it already," said the trader, saying pipeline scheduling day on Friday could be a boring affair. "I thing everything for June will be cleaned-up by Wednesday."
Cash crude markets have three days following the expiry of NYMEX futures to settle pipeline scheduling programs for the month, with June's deadline set for Friday.
The foreign delivery question has only recently appeared as a threat due to healthy premiums pegged for foreign supply.
For June, Nigerian Bonny Light holds a 60 cents premium, forcing the party delivered against to pay that premium for barrels that might not even mesh with their systems.
For July, the Bonny Light Premium will be cut to only 40 cents, alleviating some of the economic squeeze.

Overall, market fundamentals look a bit more favorable than they had. Thomas Blakeslee, analyst for Cargill Investor Services, said higher prompt prices reflected a more "accurate" reading on supply and demand over the next couple of months.
"The fundamentals are firmer than expected, and certainly part of the reason for the push higher," said Blakeslee.
Tom Bentz, head of energy trading for High Yield Analytics in New York, said North Sea maintenance and general tightness in Europe propped crude values.
"And, you have refineries in the U.S. running at high levels to keep up with demand," added Bentz.
Loadings from the eight main North Sea export terminals were expected to decline about 12.5 million barrels in June, equivalent to 260,000 barrels per day (bpd) below May.
Britain's Forties and Norway's Oseberg crudes were seen getting hit hardest by planned maintenance.

Rising U.S. inventories balance the supply equation to a degree, as well as refinery run cuts in Europe due to poor product margins. U.S. crude stocks gained some seven million barrels last week to put levels 23 million barrels above year-ago.
"How it holds $21.50 will determine if we are headed straight up from here," Bentz said, noting the trend could very well be for more expensive crude.

"Long-term stochastics, on a weekly basis, turned over into a bullish modelast week showing oversold conditions. Depending on how we hold (support), we could be in the beginning stages of a larger rally," said Bentz.
--Patrick Connole, NY Energy Desk ((+1 212 859 1620))
